The topic codes are correct as Topic 1.10 introduces the definition and Topic 1.13 covers experimental design.

The entry accurately defines a confounding variable in an observational study, matching the definition and requirements in CED 1.10.D.5: 'A confounding variable in an observational study provides an alternative explanation... To be a confounding variable, a variable must be associated with both the explanatory variable and the response variable.'

Topic 1.10, EK 1.10.D.5 states that a confounding variable in an observational study “provides an alternative explanation for the observed relationship between the explanatory and response variables” and “must be associated with both the explanatory variable and the response variable.” The entry accurately states both requirements. No caution is needed.

a_factual: The body closely follows CED 1.10.D.5. The CED says a confounding variable 'provides an alternative explanation for the observed relationship between the explanatory and response variables determined in the study.' It also says 'To be a confounding variable, a variable must be associated with both the explanatory variable and the response variable.' The entry leaves out the clause 'thereby reducing the possibility of concluding a causal relationship.' That omission does not make any stated fact wrong, and the defining condition (association with both variables) is kept exactly. b_topic_codes: Owner 1.10 is where the CED first defines a confounding variable in an observational study (1.10.D.5). Confounding in an experiment is a separate statement (1.13.A.8). Because this entry is explicitly scoped to observational studies, limiting topic_codes to 1.10 is correct. c_ced_required: LO 1.10.D ('Identify an observational study') includes EK 1.10.D.5, which requires students to apply this definition. The unit overview reinforces it: 'students need to clearly explain why a particular variable might lead to confounding in a given setting.' d_caution: The wording essentially reproduces the CED's phrasing, so no caution is needed and caution null is acceptable.
The entry accurately represents the three components of an investigative question as explicitly detailed in the CED under Topic 1.10 (Essential Knowledge 1.10.A.1, 1.10.A.2, and 1.10.A.3).

Topic 1.10.A.1–3 requires these three components in this order: the first guides data collection and names the variables of interest; the second guides the data analysis choice; and the third indicates applicable conclusions. The CED specifies the parameter and direction of the alternative for a hypothesis test, the parameter and range-estimation goal for a confidence interval, and the applicable population and, for a randomly assigned experiment, a cause-and-effect conclusion. The entry accurately paraphrases those requirements, so no caution is needed.

a_factual: All three items match the CED in content and order.
- First component: 1.10.A.1 says the first component "should guide the data collection process and should be phrased in terms of the variable(s) of interest in the study."
- Second component: 1.10.A.2 says the second component "should guide the data analysis choice." Per 1.10.A.2.i, for a hypothesis test the question should "make clear the parameter and the direction of the alternative hypothesis." Per 1.10.A.2.ii, for a confidence interval it should make clear "the parameter and the goal of estimation of that parameter within a range of potential values."
- Third component: 1.10.A.3 says the third component "should indicate the type(s) of conclusion(s) applicable from the study... the population to which the conclusions will be applicable and, in the case of an experiment that uses random assignment, a cause-and-effect conclusion."

b_topic_codes: Topic 1.10 is where the CED first breaks the investigative question into components (LO 1.10.A, "Determine the components of an investigative question within a statistical study"). Topic 1.1.B covers determining an investigative question but does not define its components. The topic_codes list contains only 1.10, which is correct.

c_ced_required: LO 1.10.A [Skill 1.A] directly requires students to determine these components.

d_caution: The entry's wording closely paraphrases the CED essential knowledge, so no caution is needed and null is acceptable.
The entry accurately represents the components of a boxplot as defined in EK 1.8.A.2. The topic codes are correct, as boxplots are introduced in Topic 1.8 and used for comparison in Topic 1.9.

Topic 1.8.A.2 first requires the boxplot and describes its box, median line, whiskers, and separately marked outliers as stated. It says that, when outliers exist, whiskers extend to the most extreme data values that are not outliers. Topic 1.9.A.1 also uses boxplots to compare distributions. No caution is needed.

a_factual: Every item matches 1.8.A.2 closely. The CED says 'The box represents the middle 50% of data, with a line at the median and the ends of the box corresponding to the quartiles.' It says 'Lines ("whiskers") that represent 25% of the data extend from the first quartile to the minimum and from the third quartile to the maximum.' It says 'If there are outliers in the data, the whiskers extend to the most extreme data values that are not outliers.' It says 'outliers are usually denoted with an asterisk or other symbol.' The body's 'graph of the five-number summary' matches 'A boxplot is a graphical representation of the five-number summary.' The body's short form 'whiskers to the extreme non-outlier values' does not contradict the CED, and the items give both the no-outlier and with-outlier cases. b_topic_codes: 1.8 is where boxplots first appear in Required Course Content (1.8.A.2). The Topic 1.5 gallery-walk mention is only an optional sample activity, and 1.5.A.1 lists only histograms, stem-and-leaf plots and dotplots. 1.9 legitimately uses boxplots: 1.9.A.1 says 'Boxplots may be used to compare center, variability, outliers, and skewness (or symmetry).' c_ced_required: 1.8.A 'Construct quantitative one-variable graphical representations of summary statistics [Skill 3.A]' together with 1.8.A.2 requires students to build and read these parts. d_caution: The wording follows the CED essentially verbatim, so no caution is needed and caution null is correct.

The entry accurately reflects the exact relationship between the mean and median under different shapes of distributions as defined in EK 1.8.B.1. The topic codes are correct, as Topic 1.8 introduces this relationship and Topic 1.9 applies comparisons of these distributions.

The body matches 1.8.B.1: for a relatively symmetric distribution, the mean and median are relatively close; for right skew, the mean is usually larger; for left skew, it is usually smaller. Topic 1.8 first requires the relationship. Topic 1.9 uses it in comparing distributions: 1.9.A.1 includes comparisons of center and skewness, and 1.9.B.1 permits comparisons using numerical summaries. No caution is needed.

a: The body matches 1.8.B.1 nearly verbatim: "If a distribution is relatively symmetric, then the values of the mean and median are relatively close to each other. If a distribution is skewed right, then the value of the mean is usually larger than the median. If the distribution is skewed left, then the value of the mean is usually smaller than the median." Both directions are correct, and the hedge "usually" is kept. b: 1.8 is where the unit first states this (LO 1.8.B, "Describe quantitative one-variable graphical representations of summary statistics based on the relationship of the mean and the median"). No earlier topic states it; 1.6 covers skew only and 1.7 covers the mean and median separately. Listing 1.9 is defensible: 1.9.B.1 says comparisons of graphical representations of summary statistics "can include any of the numerical summaries (e.g., mean, standard deviation, etc.)", and 1.9.A.1 has boxplots used to compare "skewness (or symmetry)". Reasoning about skew from the mean and median applies directly there. c: LO 1.8.B [Skill 4.A] requires students to describe distributions using this relationship, so it is required content, not textbook trivia. d: The wording matches the CED phrasing, including "relatively close" and "usually", so no caution is needed and a null caution is correct. Minor note: ced_evidence quotes only the skewed-right sentence rather than all three clauses of 1.8.B.1. It is still accurate and traceable, so this does not cause a rejection.

The entry's definition of a simple random sample (SRS) matches the CED's Essential Knowledge statement 1.11.A.3 exactly: 'In a simple random sample (SRS) of size n, every sample of the size n has the same chance of being selected.' The topic code 1.11 is correct as this is where the concept is introduced.

The body matches Topic 1.11, essential knowledge 1.11.A.3: “In a simple random sample (SRS) of size n, every sample of the size n has the same chance of being selected.” Topic 1.11 requires students to identify sampling methods; no caution is needed.

a: The body matches EK 1.11.A.3: "In a simple random sample (SRS) of size n, every sample of the size n has the same chance of being selected." The definition of bias in a sampling method is highly accurate and directly aligns with EK 1.12.A.1: 'Bias in a sampling method is a systematic error in the sampling procedure that results in a statistic being consistently larger or consistently smaller than the parameter the statistic is used to estimate.'

The definition matches 1.12.A.1: bias is a systematic error in the sampling procedure that results in a statistic being consistently larger or smaller than the parameter it is used to estimate. Topic 1.12 is the first and only listed topic for this entry. The wording needs no caution.

The body matches CED 1.12.A.1 almost word for word: "Bias in a sampling method is a systematic error in the sampling procedure that results in a statistic being consistently larger or consistently smaller than the parameter the statistic is used to estimate." The entry shortens the last phrase to "the parameter it estimates." The meaning is the same, so it is factual. 1.12 is the first place in Unit 1 that defines sampling bias, and topic_codes lists only 1.12, so the topic codes are correct. LO 1.12.A ("Identify potential sources of bias in sampling methods") requires students to know this definition. The wording is effectively the CED's own, so no caution is needed. The ced_evidence quote is truncated but accurate.

The entry perfectly aligns with LO 1.10.E (specifically EK 1.10.E.2 and 1.10.E.4) regarding when generalizations are appropriate. The caution correctly addresses the common student error of confusing random selection (for generalization) with random assignment (for cause-and-effect), which is explicitly highlighted in the 'Preparing for the AP Exam' section on page 26 of the CED.

Topic 1.10 first requires this distinction: 1.10.E.2 says random selection makes it appropriate to generalize to “the entire population ... from which the sample was selected,” while 1.10.E.4 limits generalization without random selection to “a population of individuals that are similar to those used in the study.” Topic 1.13 also uses it: 1.13.D.2 addresses the population represented by volunteer experimental units. The caution correctly distinguishes random selection from random assignment; 1.13.D.1 says random assignment allows cause-and-effect conclusions.

a_factual: The body matches the CED. 1.10.E.2 says: "When observational units, or experimental units, in a sample are randomly selected from a population, it is appropriate to make generalizations about the entire population of individuals from which the sample was selected." 1.10.E.4 says: "...not randomly selected... it is appropriate to make generalizations only about a population of individuals that are similar to those used in the study." The parenthetical "deliberately chosen or volunteers" matches 1.10.E.3: "A sample is not randomly selected when observational units are deliberately chosen or volunteer themselves to be in the sample." b_topic_codes: 1.10 is the first topic to require this (LO 1.10.E, "Justify the appropriateness of generalizations for a statistical study"). 1.13 also applies it in 1.13.D.2: "the study's experimental units are obtained from volunteers and will represent the population of experimental units similar to those who participated in the study." c_ced_required: LO 1.10.E [Skill 2.B] requires students to justify generalizations. d_caution: The caution is correct and supported by the unit overview: "Precise student answers discuss random selection when generalizing results of a sample to the population and refer to random assignment when explaining experiments or their results." It is also supported by 1.13.D.1, which ties random assignment to cause-and-effect conclusions.

The entry accurately represents the four elements of a well-designed experiment as specified in EK 1.13.A.1 (i-iv), with definitions of replication and direct control aligned with EK 1.13.A.9 and 1.13.A.10.

CED 1.13.A.1 lists, in this order, “Comparisons of at least two treatment groups,” “Random assignment of treatments to experimental units,” “Replication,” and “Direct control of potential extraneous sources of variation in the response.” CED 1.13.A.9 defines replication as assigning more than one experimental unit to each treatment, and 1.13.A.10 defines direct control as keeping settings the same from unit to unit. Topic 1.13 is where these elements are required; no caution is needed.

a_factual: The list members and their order match CED 1.13.A.1: 'A well-designed experiment should include the following: i Comparisons of at least two treatment groups, one of which could be a control group; ii Random assignment of treatments to experimental units; iii Replication; iv Direct control of potential extraneous sources of variation in the response.' The Replication meaning matches 1.13.A.9: 'more than one experimental unit is assigned to each treatment.' The Direct control gloss paraphrases 1.13.A.10: 'keeping the settings of certain potential extraneous sources of variation in the response variable the same from experimental unit to experimental unit.' The entry drops the word 'certain', which is a minor loss of precision but not a factual error. One small gap: ced_evidence cites only 1.13.A.1.i–iv, while the Replication and Direct control glosses come from 1.13.A.9–10. This is not disqualifying. b_topic_codes: Topic 1.13 'Experimental Design' is where LO 1.13.A ('Identify elements of a well-designed experiment') first appears, and it is the only listed code. c_ced_required: LO 1.13.A [Skill 2.A] directly requires students to identify these elements. d_caution: The wording is essentially CED wording, so no caution is needed.

The entry accurately reflects Essential Knowledge statement 1.12.A.6 from the AP Statistics CED, which states: 'Nonrandom sampling methods (e.g., samples chosen by convenience or voluntary response) introduce potential bias because they do not use random chance to select the individuals.' The topic code is correct and the content is directly required.

The body matches Topic 1.12, EK 1.12.A.6: “Nonrandom sampling methods (e.g., samples chosen by convenience or voluntary response) introduce potential bias because they do not use random chance to select the individuals.” Topic 1.12 is the correct owner and only listed topic. No caution is needed.

The body restates 1.12.A.6 faithfully: "Nonrandom sampling methods (e.g., samples chosen by convenience or voluntary response) introduce potential bias because they do not use random chance to select the individuals." The examples (convenience, voluntary response) and the reason (no random chance) match the CED. Topic 1.12 "Potential Problems with Sampling" is where this is first required. LO 1.12.A, "Identify potential sources of bias in sampling methods," requires students to apply it. The wording essentially matches the CED, so no caution is needed.

The entry accurately reflects the scope of conclusions from experiments as detailed in EK 1.13.D.1 and 1.13.D.2, specifically addressing the role of random assignment in establishing cause-and-effect and the limitation of using volunteer subjects to populations of similar individuals.

The substance matches 1.13.D.1: random assignment allows cause-and-effect conclusions, and 1.13.D.2: volunteer experimental units represent units similar to participants. No caution is needed. However, Topic 1.10 first requires this scope distinction: 1.10.A.3 specifies a cause-and-effect conclusion for an experiment using random assignment, and 1.10.E.4 limits generalizations from nonrandomly selected experimental units to a population similar to those studied. The owner topic should therefore be 1.10, with both 1.10 and 1.13 listed as topic codes.

The body is supported by 1.13.D.1: random assignment 'allows for cause-and-effect conclusions,' and 1.13.D.2: volunteer experimental units 'will represent the population of experimental units similar to those who participated.' No caution is needed. However, Topic 1.10 first requires this scope-of-conclusions distinction: 1.10.A.3 specifies the population to which conclusions apply and a cause-and-effect conclusion for an experiment using random assignment; 1.10.E.4 limits generalizations from units not randomly selected to individuals similar to those studied. Thus 1.13 is not the first required topic, and 1.10 is missing from topic_codes.

The entry accurately reflects EK 1.13.A.7 regarding the purpose of random assignment. The caution is highly relevant and aligns with the exam preparation advice on page 26 of the CED, which warns against confusing random selection with random assignment.

Topic 1.13.A.7 states: “The purpose of random assignment is to create treatment groups that are as similar as possible with respect to extraneous sources of variation.” It adds that, if random assignment is successful, “the respective distributions of each extraneous variable will be approximately the same for all the treatment groups.” The body reflects both statements. The caution correctly distinguishes random assignment from random selection, as the Unit 1 exam guidance does.

a_factual fails. The first clause matches 1.13.A.7: "The purpose of random assignment is to create treatment groups that are as similar as possible with respect to extraneous sources of variation." The second clause does not. The body says "so each extraneous variable's distribution is approximately the same across treatment groups," which presents balance as a guaranteed result. The CED makes it conditional: "If random assignment is successful, the respective distributions of each extraneous variable will be approximately the same for all the treatment groups." The unit overview also says random assignment only "tends to balance the effects of uncontrolled variables across groups." Dropping the "if successful" condition misstates the concept, because random assignment does not guarantee balance in any single randomization. The ced_evidence field quotes only the first sentence of 1.13.A.7, which hides this mismatch. Fix: write "if random assignment is successful, each extraneous variable's distribution will be approximately the same across treatment groups" (or "tends to make"). b passes: 1.13 is the Experimental Design topic where 1.13.A.7 appears, and it is the only topic listed. c passes: LO 1.13.A ("Identify elements of a well-designed experiment") and 1.13.D require students to apply the purpose of random assignment. d passes: the caution matches the CED's 'Preparing for the AP Exam' guidance, "some students write about random selection when the question refers to random assignment, or vice versa. Precise student answers ... refer to random assignment when explaining experiments or their results."

a: The body matches 1.13.A.7: "The purpose of random assignment is to create treatment groups that are as similar as possible with respect to extraneous sources of variation. If random assignment is successful, the respective distributions of each extraneous variable will be approximately the same for all the treatment groups." Its "as similar as possible" hedge keeps the claim from overstating, so this does not fail the check. b: The content first appears in Topic 1.13 under LO 1.13.A ("Identify elements of a well-designed experiment"), so owner 1.13 and topic_codes [1.13] are correct.
